content: Safe sanitation is a critical component of public health, playing a vital role in preventing infections and promoting mental and social well-being. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed comprehensive guidelines on sanitation and health, following the processes outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. These guidelines aim to maximize the health benefits of sanitation interventions by providing evidence-based recommendations and practical guidance for international, national, and local sanitation policies and programs. The guidelines emphasize the importance of safe sanitation systems, which are designed to separate human excreta from human contact at all stages of the sanitation service chain. This includes toilet capture, containment, emptying, transport, treatment (either on-site or off-site), and final disposal or end use. Such systems must meet safety requirements while respecting human rights and addressing associated hygiene practices and essential services. The target audience for these guidelines includes national and local authorities responsible for the safety of sanitation systems and services, such as policymakers, planners, and implementers within and outside the health sector. These stakeholders are tasked with developing, implementing, and monitoring sanitation standards and regulations. The guidelines also highlight the role of health authorities in identifying and managing health risks related to sanitation. The evidence reviewed during the development of these guidelines indicates that safe sanitation is associated with significant health improvements, including reductions in infectious diseases, better nutrition, and enhanced well-being. However, the quality of evidence is often limited due to challenges in conducting randomized controlled trials and the variability in study settings, interventions, and outcomes. Despite these limitations, the guidelines provide actionable recommendations to address these gaps and improve sanitation systems globally. Key recommendations include prioritizing universal access to toilets that safely contain excreta, eliminating open defecation, and ensuring equitable progress in line with the human right to water and sanitation. Governments are encouraged to address both the demand and supply of sanitation facilities to promote adoption and sustained use. Community-wide coverage with safe toilets is essential, and shared or public facilities can serve as incremental steps when individual household toilets are not feasible. Health authorities are urged to play a central role in coordinating sanitation efforts across multiple sectors, developing sanitation norms and standards, and including sanitation in health policies and surveillance systems. To support implementation, the guidelines outline good practices such as defining government-led, multi-sectoral sanitation policies, ensuring health risk management is reflected in legislation and standards, and enabling the marketing and development of sanitation services and business models. Local health-based risk assessments should be conducted to prioritize improvements and manage system performance effectively. Safe sanitation systems must meet minimum safety requirements at each step of the sanitation service chain. The WHO guidelines on sanitation and health aim to provide practical tools and resources for ministries, health authorities, and implementers to make informed investments in sanitation interventions that yield the best possible health outcomes for all.
